title: Evercrest Consulting — Model path, context length, and VPC needs (discovery)
summary: Discovery call to understand Evercrest's product constraints and model choices. Customer has heavy multi-document context needs (long conversations and documents up to ~40k tokens), requires Spanish + French support, and is leaning toward a private VPC deployment due to client data residency. Discussed open model tradeoffs, tool-calling for internal search/DB calls, and latency vs cost profiles for hosted vs dedicated capacity.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-06-16 16:00 PDT
Duration: 58 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Jordan Miles (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), John Alvarez (Evercrest CTO), Mia Gomez (Product), Victor Lee (Data Eng)
Links shared: Redwood model comp deck https://redwood.ai/decks/evercrest-models , security/architectural notes https://redwood.ai/security/handbook (shared in chat)

[00:00] Jordan: ok hi everyone, thanks for joining, we uh we have about an hour, i'm jordan from redwood inference, with priya who is our solutions engineer, ready to dig into models and infra, over to you john for a quick kickoff?

[00:22] John: yeah thanks jordan, um overview — Evercrest is building a document synthesis product for enterprise legal teams, they ingest contracts, deposition notes, email threads, lots of long documents, so context length is the big thing for us. we're also shipping to EU clients so data residency and VPC is pretty important.

[00:45] Priya: great, that helps, are you primarily evaluating open models or also considering hosted proprietary endpoints?

[00:53] Mia: We're leaning open models for cost and auditability, but we'll consider hosted if it means less ops. Key requirements: 1) handle 30k-40k token context occasionally, 2) strong Spanish and French responses with legal terminology, 3) ability to call our internal search and RDBMS via tool-calls, and 4) audit logs / KMS integration for keys.

[01:20] Jordan: super clear. So there are three axes we typically look at: model capability (LLM choice and quantization), runtime/deployment (hosted vs dedicated vs private VPC/on-prem), and operational features (tool-calling, KV cache, rollouts). We'll map those to your SLOs.

[01:43] Victor: two practical questions up front — latency target is sub-800ms for short queries, but long-context batch jobs can be minutes. also budget: we need to keep token cost predictability for enterprise clients, so reserved capacity might be interesting.

[02:05] Priya: good, so for short-turn conversational queries hosted API with a smaller model or cached prefixes can meet sub-second latencies. For your 30k-40k contexts we typically recommend a dedicated or private deployment because you can attach specialized kernels and >32k context variants and control NVMe for KV (K V) caches. We can quantify that in a bench.

[02:36] John: can you walk through open model tradeoffs — we've been reading about Mistral, Llama-2-Chat, MPT, and a couple of newer 32k models. Which ones hold up for legal domain and multilingual?

[02:52] Priya: sure — quick high level: Llama-2-chat (variants) are solid generalists, lots of community tooling, but for long context you want a 32k-capable checkpoint or sliding window approaches. Mistral (when available in 32k) tends to be more token-efficient in generation but may need domain finetune. MPT-family has good long-context options (some custom kernel work needed). Also newer open 32k models are emerging — they vary in safety filters and hallucination characteristics. For legal you often want a conservatively tuned model or to pair with retrieval and stronger prompt engineering.

[03:35] Mia: retrieval plus tool-calling is key — we want the model to ask to call a search tool rather than hallucinate. do you support function/tool-calling patterns?

[03:45] Jordan: yes — Redwood supports structured tool-calling patterns, similar to function calling, and we have patterns for safe retrieval calls. You can register tool schemas, and the runtime will surface those calls to your service. There's also a fallback policy if tool fails, so you don't get garbage.

[04:10] Victor: any limits on parallel tool calls or rate limiting for heavy workloads?

[04:15] Priya: you configure that per-route; with Dedicated you get predictable throughput and can reserve concurrency (autoscale policies). Hosted has quotas and burst policies. For private VPC you control the network egress and tooling, and we provide metrics for concurrency and queue depth.

[04:40] John: security — we need SOC2, audit logs, KMS, and possibly customer-managed keys, plus SAML SSO integration and RBAC. How mature is Redwoods enterprise security?

[04:52] Jordan: Redwood is SOC2 compliant, we support KMS integrations and can do customer-managed keys in the Private offering, SAML/SSO and SCIM for user provisioning, and per-token tracing in the console. I'll attach our security pack after the call.

[05:10] Mia: great, also data residency: EU clients want data to stay in eu-west and not cross regions. can we pin region?

[05:18] Priya: yes — Hosted can pin to region depending on model availability, Dedicated gives region guarantees for reserved capacity, and Private obviously lets you run inside your VPC/air-gapped environment. There are tradeoffs: private gives you max control but increases ops and cost.

[05:40] John: can you run on-prem for really sensitive clients?

[05:44] Jordan: we offer on-prem packages for top-tier enterprise customers, including a private control plane and options to run inference on customer hardware. It requires a procurement cycle and entailed support, but we have precedents.

[06:00] Victor: let's dig into latency vs cost with longer contexts — what's the typical cost delta between hosted quantized models and dedicated 8-bit or 4-bit setups?

[06:10] Priya: rough ballpark: in hosted for standard 8k contexts using quantized open models you see lower per-token ops but because of shared infra bursts can be costlier at scale. Dedicated allows you to use aggressive quantization and kernel optimization — that can cut per-token GPU costs substantially (20-50% depending on workload). For 32k contexts you're also paying for memory and nvme-backed kv caches, so plan for a premium but you gain determinism. We'll run a modeled estimate for your usage.

[06:45] John: any native KV cache or prefix caching? we often re-query similar contract prefixes.

[06:50] Priya: yes — Redwood has prefix and KV caching, automatic reuse of cached keys between requests when the prefix matches. That greatly reduces cost for repetitive contexts. We also expose tuning knobs.

[07:06] Mia: multilingual quality — do you recommend fine-tuning or prompt engineering? Spanish legal is tricky for us.

[07:13] Priya: both. Start with retrieval augmented generation tuned prompts and a small in-domain fine-tune or LoRA on representative Spanish legal docs. Then monitor quality with our eval harness. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization and model variants based on evals.

[07:34] Victor: what about hallucination mitigation — can we force citations or return structured evidence?

[07:39] Jordan: yes, you can require the model to provide evidence snippets from the retrieval layer and set hard constraints (tool calls instead of free text). We also have structured output enforcement for JSON-schema-like responses.

[08:00] John: ok let's talk concrete pilot — we'd like a POC that demonstrates: 1) 32k-context retrieval workflow with Spanish docs, 2) tool-calling to our search API, 3) region pinned to eu-west. expected timeline 6–8 weeks. does that sound reasonable?

[08:18] Priya: absolutely, typical POC looks like 4–8 weeks depending on integration work. For the 32k part we can either use a 32k-compatible open checkpoint in Dedicated, or run a sliding-window retrieval strategy in Hosted to emulate longer context while we bake the private deployment. We'll outline the tradeoffs in the POC plan.

[08:40] John: what metrics do you recommend we measure during the POC?

[08:44] Priya: latency P95, token cost per session, retrieval precision/recall, per-route error rates, and hallucination incidents per 1k prompts. Also track cost per end-user session to compare to your pricing expectations.

[09:05] Mia: procurement questions — typical lead time for Dedicated or Private?

[09:10] Jordan: Dedicated you can reserve in weeks if capacity available; Private/on-prem is months and requires contracts. We'll flag that in the timeline.

[09:22] Victor: any competitors' gotchas we should be aware of? we've heard Anthropic is strong on safety but costy, huggingface has flexible hosting but edgeless infra ops.

[09:33] Jordan: right — Anthropic tends to be safety-forward, OpenAI has strong models but closed, huggingface is great for model agility but you manage infra. Redwood aims to combine runtime performance with ops controls so you get predictable economics with less infra build.

[09:55] John: sample ask — can you run a small benchmark on a 20-document contract set to show latency and token cost for: (A) Hosted Llama-variant w/ sliding retrieval, (B) Dedicated 32k open model, (C) Private on-prem 32k?

[10:12] Priya: yes we'll scope that. We'll need the artifact and sample queries; prefer you drop them in a secure S3 link or share via your vault. We'll also need a list of Spanish legal terms you care about for evals.

[10:28] Mia: noted, we'll prepare.

[10:32] Jordan: quick recap — action items and next steps after this call, we'll summarize in the email.

[10:40] Priya: i'll run the bench plan and draft the POC scope. jordan will send pricing and security docs. customer to share sample contracts, search API spec, and desired evaluation terms.

[10:55] John: cool thanks, we'll get those to you by end of next week.

[11:00] Jordan: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with a calendar invite for a scoping session and the POC plan.

End of transcript (approx 58 minutes).
